Treatment effect on annual income before validity adjustments (Workers in rural Bangladesh)
rows.explainer:
Estimate from a regression using publicly available THRIVE data, where the main outcome is monthly income (self-reported). We assume that the effect on monthly income is representative of the effect on annual income.

Regression details:
To deal with upper-end outliers in the income data, we first winsorize the income data at the 99th percentile. We then run a linear regression of endline income against treatment group, controlling for all other baseline variables in the dataset. We do this to reduce any bias that may be introduced by dropping observations with missing outcome data. This yields a treatment effect estimate of approx. $13, relative to a control group endline (winsorized) income mean of approx. $60. ~$13 / ~$60 = 21.3%.

The treatment effect estimates are robust to the selection and form of control group variables. Quantile regression using the raw (non-winsorized) outcome

rows.label: Adjustment for unblinded self-reporting of income (Workers in rural Bangladesh)
rows.explainer:
Guess at the extent to which self-reported income, in a trial where participants were not blind to the treatment, inflates the estimated treatment effect.

"Weaknesses must also be acknowledged: the trial’s main and secondary outcomes were both self-reported, and the investigators did not feel that participant masking with sham glasses was ethical in this setting. Thus, the potential for placebo effects cannot be excluded." Sehrin et al 2024, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0296115.

Adjustment to account for lower proportion of recipients involved in near-vision intensive economic activity relative to study, due to inability to screen for t
rows.explainer:
Sehrin et al report challenges in meeting their target sample size using only those involved in near-vision intensive occupations. We'd expect this challenge to be larger at scale.

In addition, we expect that in practice there may be some misreporting of occupation during the screening process, and/or that implementers will be unwilling to turn away people who need eyeglasses but do not work in a near-vision intensive occupation.

We are unsure about the size of this adjustment and would seek further evidence or ways to triangulate the adjustment prior to making grants to this type of program.

"In order to complete the target sample size, it was also necessary to include a moderate number (432, 52.4% of the total sample) of persons with less near vision-intensive occupations, resulting in a study cohort enriched for visually-demanding work." Sehrin et al 2024, https://doi.org/10.1371/j

rows.label: Adjustment to account for difference in distribution mechanism in non-trial context (Workers in rural Bangladesh)
rows.explainer:
Sehrin et al study used door-to-door delivery. We've heard from multiple implementers that delivery at a camp or other more public setting can be more effective at generating eyeglass use because it helps create a more salient social norm of eyeglass use. The size of this adjustment is a subjective guess.

"Based on the census, door-to-door visits was conducted to get the data of persons over and above of 40 years of age. We received a pool of eligible participants for the study." Sehrin et al. 2024, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0296115

rows.label: Adjustment to account for seasonality in the average income effect (Workers in rural Bangladesh)
rows.explainer:
In Sehrin et al, participants were followed up 8 months after the intervention, but the question asked only about income in the past 4 weeks, which may not be representative of incomes (and the effect of income) over a whole year. We suspect that there is some seasonality in income and the effect of the program, and that the study authors may have avoided running the trial at a time of year when incomes (and hence the measured effect of the intervention) were expected to be relatively low. Since we do not have direct evidence that this is the case, we apply only a small downward adjustment.

"The primary trial outcome was the between-group difference in change in monthly income (self-reported in Bangladeshi taka over the past 4 weeks) between baseline and follow-up surveys." Sehrin et al 2024, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0296115

rows.label: Adjustment to account for smaller productivity gains in non-trial contexts (Workers in rural Bangladesh)
rows.explainer:
We think there are also other factors that might make the effect size larger in an RCT than a program at scale. 

For example, workers who know they are being studied might work harder, and it's possible that near-vision impairment mainly limits productivity among workers who are already motivated to work efficiently. If so, workers with visual impairment who are less motivated would experience less of a benefit from receiving eyeglasses. Thus, if workers in non-trial contexts are less motivated, they may not receive the same level of productivity benefit as the RCT participants.

The magnitude of this adjustment is a subjective guess.

rows.explainer: GiveWell reports this model's result in multiples of cash transfers. Multiplying by GiveWell's value of a dollar to GiveDirectly converts it into units of value per dollar, so it ranks against the other models. Older sheets used older moral weights; the multiple of cash is the comparable number across years.
